title: Cognitive Debt - Why AI makes human judgment the bottleneck

segments.text: Can you please give an end of the day huge round of applause for Alissa? >> [applause] >> Hi everyone. I'll start right away. Because I believe there is a gap in the
AI story we tell. At least the story that I encounter. With one prompt you can generate a Technics illusion. You can build yourself an army of agents
and replace entire teams. Speed has been placed into our hands and speed is now the default. Now I'm not saying this out of a
skeptical distance. I'm fascinated by AI. Like many of you here, I'm part of the AI hype. But nonetheless and even more so, I was
wondering whether AI is taking work off our hands. So beginning of the year I was in an AI tunnel you could say. I built my own
product, the Empfinderei, an app to learn how to express your emotions and use it in your day-to-day. I used Lovable as my main platform. I
had ChatGPT and Claude assisting me because I'm no software developer. And I was excited on how fast I was moving. But at the same time, I felt mentally
saturated. I had days where I felt dizzy. Because I believe the effort didn't vanish. It moved from producing myself to checking, correcting, making decisions.
And we talk about AI as if things are becoming effortless. But I believe the effort is moving into areas the productivity language has now
vocabulary for. So last year Meter, a AI lab evaluating AI, did a field study with experienced developers working on a real code base with fully integrated AI.
And before they were working on the tasks, they were asked what they would expect. And they expected to be 24% faster. But in reality, they were 19% slower.
Now, I'm not saying AI is slowing us down. That's not the final word. But the expectation gap is too big to ignore. So the question is, why?
And my thesis is the bottleneck is no longer information. It is the human capacity to turn information into judgment. And when we design work as if judgment
scales at the same pace as AI does, we create cognitive depth. And cognitive depth, in my own words, is when we move faster at the surface while
underneath the human carries the judgment load. Because we all know AI can generate more than we can comfortably evaluate. And the hard part is not from moving
from the first version, but it is judging the first version and if it's any good. So for the next 20 minutes, I will focus
uh on three main parts. How AI is change our cognitive structure, why it creates new forms of mental load, and what you can do as leaders and maybe
HR practitioners to protect judgment. And first we have to look how work has moved. And this might not be new, but I still want to frame it.
Because so far the AI narrative has been AI will replace our work. And I don't believe that's true, but work is now asking something different
of us. Before AI, we were producers. And we basically drafted the concepts ourself. And we owned the context, we executed the fine task, and held the individual
focus. But now we are supervisors. We are reviewing the candidates AI presents us. We check the assumptions, we hold the human context inside those models, and
we exercise judgment. And judgment is no lighter than execution. It maybe needs less typing, yes, but it demands more of us. And that is the first layer of cognitive
depth. Because the work looks lighter on the surface, but the judgment load underneath increases. Now, what does judgment actually run on as I'm talking about cognitive
capacities? There are three main pillars that we use when we practice judgment. One attention. So, we concentrate on specific information AI provides us. Not only does this look right, but does
it also fit the situation and the purpose? Second, our working memory. So, we hold and manipulate information. We build version, we build constraints. And third, and that's probably the most
difficult for all of us, inhibition. So, we have to that that is the restraint to prevent to act upon impulses. So, to resist the plausible but wrong
answer. And judgment tasks put all three of those cognitive capacities under load simultaneously. And therefore, my statement is you are no longer producing the work,
but you are reviewing a machine's version of thinking. And that feels like an upgrade for many. But cognitively, it's very demanding. We hold the full mental model while
evaluating confident but maybe wrong output. And we do so under volume and under time pressure, which is one of the most demanding jobs our brain can do.
Now, you might say, "Well, AI does make me faster and more productive." And I would not disagree. Because for repetitive work and low judgment work, I believe AI can
definitely be a huge support. But the real question should also not be whether AI is making us more productive, but more productive at what?
At producing output? Yes, definitely. But does AI support us in making better judgments? That's a different claim. And there is some evidence into the direction that our perceived
productivity increases with one to two and also to three AI tools. But then it dips. And three is not a magical number, but it shows us that we humans have a limit
on how much we can cognitively hold and supervise. And that this is another layer of cognitive depth. So we increase the output faster than we increase the human capacity to
supervise it. Now, 275 interruptions. That's a number from Microsoft's Work Trend Index from last year. Workers experience up to 275 interruptions a day. Now, disclaimer, this is not an average
number. You could say this is a heavy user. So someone in a high communicative and high volume environment. But we all know how many interruptions
we face in our day-to-day. So it's not about the exact number, but the pattern behind it. And Gloria Mark is a researcher in the
field of interruptions at work. And she found out that people who are interrupted work faster, which is a surprise. But they do so because they compensate.
And after 20 minutes of interrupted work, the stress level increased significantly. You have an experience of frustration and time pressure. So work gets done with a cost.
Complex work requires you to hold a full mental model. And every interruption is a reload cost. You have to reload and re-architect the model you just had in your mind.
And therefore, cognitive depth compounds. AI increases the amount that we have to supervise, while our work environments are reducing the attention that we need
to supervise it well. So, BCG and Harvard Business Review did a study. They wanted to find out how people work with AI. And they coined the term AI brain fry.
Participants described it as buzzing, a fog in their mind, like a mental hangover. And it describes a very specific workplace pattern. The mental fatigue resulting from
excessive use of AI beyond one's cognitive capacity. Now, the irony is that AI was supposed to take off our mental burden. But for many people, we experience an
additional, a new kind of mental burden. And that is the burden of supervision. It was also the most taxing factor for AI brain fry. Oversight, monitoring AI,
correcting AI, making decisions, including the context. And the second important factor was that everything was happening on top of everything else. Work did not get
reduced. So, this builds up. Now, the pattern does not stop here, because those who experienced AI brain fry, they were also more likely to quit.
There was a higher intent to quit by 34%. Because it is about whether we as people can work in an environment without burning our cognitive capacities. Those
capacities that we depend on when we work now with AI. And therefore the question is, what happens when the people making the most important decisions are doing so
under constant cognitive load? Because if my statement is correct, if judgment is the bottleneck, then cognitive load isn't personal. It's a systems issue. And therefore we also have to reflect on
the system that we use um to do judging, our human brain. And there are three main areas that are especially important for the work that
we're doing. Because judgment isn't abstract, it runs on our nervous system. And our nervous system needs certain operating conditions. Our prefrontal cortex, which is
basically our executive control center, where we prioritize, plan, inhibit, that's basically the area doing most of the judgment work. But it basically has a sister or
brother, you could say, the amygdala, our threat detection area. And then we have the hippocampus, who holds especially short-term memory, so every decision that you're making
throughout the day, and is responsible for learning. Now, under stress and sustained load, it gets less reliable. Our brain moves from being triggered by
urgency and is therefore not as functional when it comes to complexity. Our prefrontal cortex becomes less reliable and therefore it is harder for us to prioritize, inhibit and inhibit
the plausible but wrong answer. The amygdala becomes more reactive and therefore we faster at making decisions and less patient in understanding the full context.
And the hippocampus has a very hard time to hold the context. So we lose threat especially if we're interrupted. So again, if judgement is the
bottleneck, then stress and fragmentation are not just well-being issue. They change the quality of the judgement that we're doing. So I want to move to the practical part of
this talk now, which is basically my statement that cognitive endurance is built through rhythm, load and recovery. As I mentioned, it is a design
constraint to design those working conditions. And I'm not saying use less AI. I'm saying use AI in a way without straining your cognitive capacity.
And I'm going to show you three principles not as a universal truth but as food for thought. First, guard your focus. Now you might smirk because this is not
a new principle. But with everything that I've shown you now, every interruption disrupts the mental model. And it has a cost to reconstruct it.
And many people of us spend most of their work time in a rather shallow or reactive mode. So, therefore, fix it. Block 60 to 90 minutes in your calendar,
notifications off, and build yourself real working conditions. The quality of judgment inside that working block will be different than the judgment you're making in a fragmented
day. Now, I may be also talking to leaders and I want to talk to you directly because this is a team decision. It's not an individual discipline.
Without organizational support, this focus becomes fragile. So, therefore, design it in. The second principle is think first, AI second. And before I explain that, I want to
invite you in to think of a real problem you're facing right now. This can be a tense stakeholder relationship or a difficult decision you're have you have to make when you
return back to work. Whatever it might be, a real problem, and just hold it for 10 seconds in your mind. Now imagine three AI answers already arrived on your
desk. All those answers are similar, but slightly different. At the same time, your phone pings and your colleague interrupts you with just a quick
question. That is basically your working memory under load. That is the friction you experience in your day-to-day. And if you prompt before thinking, you outsource the problem framing.
You become the reviewer of a machine-generated problem frame that you haven't fully formed yet. And for simple task, that's fine. But for non-trivial task where stakes
are involved, there is a risk. And therefore, my um recommendation would be to practice your own problem framing first. Write down three bullet points, a
sentence, a decision tree on a posted note, whatever works for you. And then use one AI. I believe your prompt will get better, but I also believe it will be easier for
you to review the output. And you train your judgment. You do not let AI replace it. Now, the third principle is keep context in the loop.
Because as we all know, AI makes messy things sound very manageable. And sometimes that's helpful because it's frictionless and it's smooth in terms of communication.
But sometimes that's exactly the trouble, especially when people are involved. Because where written isn't context-aware. It ignores power dynamics or this long overdue decision that broke trust.
And the language looks neutral, but the situation is not. And what concerns me here isn't that AI misses it. Because AI has no link to the history.
AI has no link to the real world. My concern is that we miss it and that we do not involve the human context that is necessary for those
situations. And that's atrophy. We stop practicing the judgment muscle that is needed nowadays to make good judgment calls. So, therefore, start including context. The social context, the cultural
context, the ethical context, but also the consequences that maybe someone needs to bear if things go wrong. And therefore, before I close off this
talk, I want to put my argument plainly. The job changed. It moved from producing to judgment, and this is already happening. This is not a
prediction. Judgment runs on attention, on our working memory. We have to hold complex models in our mind, and stress and fragmentation make that less reliable.
This is a strategic issue. It's not a well-being issue. So, maybe don't ask whether AI can make us faster, but rather where does judgment matter
most. Because if we do not design for this change, we accumulate cognitive debt until it shows up in decisions that were done badly, in people technically present but
running on empty, and in attrition that we did not expect. And therefore, my final words are in the age AI age, your brain is not a soft
asset. It's the system that decides what becomes real. And therefore, treat it like capital and invest in it accordingly. And here is where I say thank you for
coming and >> [applause]
